title: Provincial development charge reduction grant application
subtitle: Risks to taxpayers, housing types affected, and closed-session direction on grant negotiations and a Habitat for Humanity receivable.
overview: Council held a special summer meeting to respond to the province's Development Charge Reduction Program. It endorsed the City's grant application, which staff had already submitted by the June 19 deadline. Council also approved setting up a Residential Development Charge Reduction Grant, but only if the application succeeds and a transfer payment agreement is signed {{vote:m1}}.

If funded, the City would charge development charges at the full rate and apply a temporary grant equal to 30 percent of the residential charge for three years. The grant would pay for three water and wastewater growth projects. Staff said the main risk is that building activity could exceed the funded estimate, leaving a gap paid through property taxes and utility rates. Lower activity could lead the province to claw back funding.

The province has not yet said whether the application was successful. A possible restricted acts period starting August 21 means an agreement may have to be signed under the CAO's delegated authority. Council met in closed session on negotiation parameters, the grant agreement and a Habitat for Humanity development charges receivable. After the session, the mayor reported that council gave direction to staff on all three items.

decisions.detail: Council endorsed the City's application to the Development Charge Reduction Program through the Ministry of Housing and Municipal Affairs and received the staff report.
Council approved creating a Residential Development Charge Reduction Grant, subject to a successful application and an executed transfer payment agreement.

debate: Several councillors asked what happens if the program goes badly. Staff said the cost is the charge otherwise owed times 30 percent for every unit built in the three years, and any amount above the grant would fall on taxes and rates. Staff said they tried to limit this risk by basing the request on an ambitious development estimate.

One councillor asked about guarantees that savings would reach buyers, and staff said there are none. Another said the risks sit with the City while the returns go to developers. Staff pointed to infrastructure funding and housing growth as benefits to the City. The mayor said developers had indicated that competition would pass savings on to buyers.

Councillors questioned whether the build estimate is realistic. Staff acknowledged that the roughly 5,000 units needed to use up the grant is much higher than past activity in Guelph. The mayor said they did not expect that many units to be built in three years. Councillors also raised workforce limits and competition with other municipalities for trades, which staff said were not specifically factored in.

Some councillors raised the compressed timeline and the lack of any response from the province. Staff said the application window was about two weeks for work that normally takes many months. Only Toronto had received a funding announcement.

Councillors asked what types of housing would benefit, since the program cannot target particular types. Staff reported the pipeline is mostly apartments and multi-residential buildings, with few single-detached homes. One councillor supported the application but said municipalities still need sustained infrastructure funding from senior governments.
